the evidence gathered here supports that review.","performanceTask":"Shared Stories, Shared Lessons asks students to compare texts, analyze values and adaptations, and use evidence from multiple sources; today's discussion practice builds that spoken evidence and cross-text comparison."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"retelling","definition":"a new version of an older story","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"adaptation","definition":"a version of a story changed for a new form, such as a film made from a novel","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"omit","definition":"to leave out","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"perspective","definition":"a way of seeing or thinking about something; a point of view","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"discourse marker","definition":"a word or phrase that connects ideas when speaking, such as 'for example' or 'on the other hand'","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"faithful","definition":"staying close to the original","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"evidence","definition":"details from a text that support an idea","tier":"support"},{"word":"formal","definition":"serious, appropriate language for school","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"Chapters and pages students choose as discussion evidence (e.g., Ch. 18, pp. 283-291; Ch. 22, pp. 354-369)"},{"title":"Myths from Investigations 1 and 2 (including Virgil's Aeneid and Homer's Odyssey excerpts)","author":"Various"},{"title":"Teacher-chosen film clips of The Lightning Thief","author":"Various"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students quickly name where they are in their discussion preparation so the teacher can form responsive Huddles.","activities":[{"id":"launch-discussion-check-in","title":"Discussion Check-In","minutes":5,"standards":[],"routine":"Reflection","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Rate yourself from 1 to 4 with your fingers on each statement: (1) I have a clear idea about how retellings change. (2) I have a text or film detail ready as evidence. (3) I can use a discourse marker to connect my ideas."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Last time we began our discussion about how retellings change across cultures and generations. Today is a catch-up day. I will meet with small groups while everyone else keeps working. Show me your ratings."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which part feels hardest: finding evidence, explaining your idea, or connecting it to someone else's idea?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Connecting to someone else's idea is hardest for me. I know what I think, but I forget to say 'building on what you said' and I just start talking about my own point."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Use ratings and your notes from Lesson 35 to sort students: Huddle 1 for students rating 1-2 on statement 2 (evidence), Huddle 2 for 1-2 on statement 3 (discussion language), Huddle 3 for 1-2 on statement 1 (ideas about novel and film). Students not in a Huddle keep preparing or hold a make-up discussion in pairs."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Three short Huddles reteach what the Arc built: citing evidence, comparing versions of a story, and using academic language in discussion. Students not in a Huddle finish their discussion work independently.","activities":[{"id":"huddle-1-evidence","title":"Huddle 1: Evidence from the Novel and Myths","minutes":14,"standards":[],"routine":"Huddle","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Pull students who have no specific detail ready. Others work independently. Option 1: rehearse a 30-second point with evidence for the discussion with a partner. Option 2: write one sentence comparing the novel and a myth, such as Chapter 22 and Odyssey Book 13 or Chapter 21 and Iliad Book 1. You do not need to run all three Huddles; focus on the need your data shows."},{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"A chapter students chose as evidence (e.g., Chapter 18, pp. 283-291, the 'NO LIVING' sign and lobby)"},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"**Reteach.** Strong discussion evidence is a specific detail (a quote, action, or image) plus a sentence explaining what it shows. In Lessons 25 and 26 students used the 'NO LIVING' sign and the guard's dialogue to show how Riordan modernizes the Underworld compared with Virgil."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"A discussion point needs a detail from the text. Saying 'Riordan changes the myth' is a claim. The 'NO LIVING' sign in the Underworld lobby is evidence. Today we connect the two."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Pick a scene you want to use in the discussion. What is one specific detail from it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In Chapter 18 the Underworld entrance has a sign that says 'NO LIVING' and a guard in a lobby, like an office building."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does that detail show about how the retelling changed the older story?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It shows Riordan made death feel modern and bureaucratic, with signs and security. In the Aeneid the crossing is dark and awe-inspiring, so the new version is funnier and more familiar to readers today."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How could you say that out loud using a discourse marker?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"For example, in Chapter 18 the sign says 'NO LIVING,' which shows Riordan updates the Underworld with modern ideas, whereas Virgil's version feels ancient and gloomy."},{"type":"directions","text":"Quick Check: Write one spoken-style point for the discussion with three parts: a claim, a detail from the novel or a myth, and a sentence that explains what the detail shows."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Spot-check that each student names a specific detail and explains it rather than only retelling the plot."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students connect a specific text detail to an idea about retellings when speaking.","sayAsk":"Say: 'One detail that shows this is...' Ask: 'Which words in the book tell you that?' Frames: 'In Chapter ___, the author describes ___.' 'This is different from the myth because ___.' Reframe: 'You said \"it's modern\"; we can say: \"Riordan modernizes the Underworld by adding a lobby and a guard.\"'","watchFor":"If a student retells without a detail, then ask 'Show me the line in the book.' If a student names a detail without explaining it, then offer 'This shows that...' Success: the student names a detail and finishes the explanation sentence orally."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding a detail to use","tryThis":"Give the student a page range and have them find one image, quote, or action that surprised them, then use the frame 'One detail is ___.'"},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Have the student pair a detail from the novel with a detail from a myth and explain what each shows about its culture or generation."}]}]},{"id":"huddle-2-discussion-language","title":"Huddle 2: Language of Academic Discussion","minutes":13,"standards":[],"routine":"Huddle","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Pull students who speak in short, informal statements or do not connect to peers' ideas. Others work independently: Option 1 write two discourse markers they plan to use and a sentence for each; Option 2 write a question to ask a partner about the film or a myth."},{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"Chapter 22, pp. 354-369, and Odyssey Book 13 excerpt (the two homecomings from Lesson 34)"},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"**Reteach.** Discourse markers show how ideas connect: to add (also, building on), to give evidence (for example, according to the text), to contrast (however, on the other hand), to disagree politely (I see it differently because). Formal wording uses precise words such as retelling, adaptation, omit, perspective, faithful."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In a good discussion, we do not only share our ideas; we link them to each other. Discourse markers are the bridges. Let's practice with Percy's choice in Chapter 22 and Odysseus's homecoming."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How could you contrast Percy's homecoming with Odysseus's using a discourse marker?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Odysseus is trying to return to his kingdom, whereas Percy chooses to go back to his mom and live at camp in the summer. On the other hand, both of them are deciding where home is."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"A classmate says, 'The book keeps the myth the same.' How could you respectfully respond?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I see it a little differently. For example, Riordan omits the gods' long speeches and adds modern details like cell phones, so the retelling is not very faithful to the original."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which sentence sounds more formal: 'The movie is kinda different' or 'The adaptation omits several events from the novel'? Why?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The second one sounds more formal because it uses exact words like adaptation and omits. 'Kinda different' is vague and sounds like talking to a friend."},{"type":"directions","text":"Quick Check: Say aloud to your partner a two-sentence contribution that uses one discourse marker and one vocabulary word (retelling, adaptation, omit, perspective, or faithful). Your partner responds with a different discourse marker."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Listen for markers used accurately (a contrast marker for a contrast), not just inserted. Have students reread their notes aloud once at a steady pace before speaking."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Give students sentence frames and models so they can add to, contrast, and politely challenge ideas in discussion.","sayAsk":"Say: 'Building on what you said...' 'For example, the text says...' 'I see it differently because...' Ask: 'Which word connects your idea to your partner's idea?' Reframe: 'You said \"no, wrong\"; we can say: \"I see it differently because the novel shows...\"' Have students say each frame chorally, then with a partner.","watchFor":"If a student uses only 'and' to connect ideas, then offer a marker menu (however, for example, in contrast). If a student uses a marker that does not fit the idea, then ask 'Are you adding or contrasting?' Success: the student uses a fitting marker and a vocabulary word in a complete spoken sentence."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: starting a contribution","tryThis":"Give a printed card of three frames and let the student rehearse one with you before speaking to a partner."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask the student to paraphrase a partner's point, then add a contrasting point that uses evidence from a different text or the film."}]}]},{"id":"huddle-3-novel-and-film","title":"Huddle 3: Comparing the Novel and the Film","minutes":13,"standards":[],"routine":"Huddle","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Pull students who are unsure what changed in the film or why it matters. Others work independently: Option 1 list two details the film omits or changes from a chapter they know; Option 2 write one sentence explaining whether the film is faithful or not."},{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief and teacher-chosen film clip","pages":"A chapter students know well (e.g., Chapter 20, pp. 320-333, or the Gateway Arch battle in Chapter 13) and the matching clip"},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"**Reteach.** An adaptation changes a story for a new form and audience. Writers and filmmakers omit, add, or change details, which changes tone and perspective. In Lesson 29 students contrasted Chapter 20 dialogue with the film dialogue; in Lesson 20 they looked at how Riordan modernizes a battle through setting and humor."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Remember, a retelling is never exactly the same. Our job in the discussion is to name one change, give evidence from the book and the film, and explain why it matters."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is one thing the film omits or changes compared with the novel?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In the novel, Percy narrates in a funny, first-person voice, but in the film we only see events and hear no narration, so we miss his thoughts about his mom."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does that change affect the viewer's perspective on the story?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In the book we see everything through Percy's eyes, so we feel his worry and humor. In the film we see more from the outside, so the story feels more like an action movie and less personal."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Would you call this adaptation faithful? What evidence supports your answer?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I would say it is only partly faithful. It keeps the main quest, but it omits Percy's narration and changes the dialogue between Percy and Annabeth, so the theme of trust feels weaker."},{"type":"directions","text":"Quick Check: Write or say one comparison sentence about the novel and the film. Include one detail from each, a discourse marker, and a word such as omit, perspective, or faithful."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Check that students compare actual details from the text and the clip, not opinions like 'the book is better.' Prompt for a reason behind the change."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in comparing two versions of a story using precise academic language.","sayAsk":"Say: 'In the novel, ___, but in the film, ___.' 'The film omits ___, which changes ___.' 'This adaptation is / is not faithful because ___.' Ask: 'What did you see in the clip? What did you read in the book?' Reframe: 'You said \"the movie is different\"; we can say: \"The film omits Percy's narration.\"'","watchFor":"If a student gives an opinion only, then ask 'What detail from the book or film shows that?' If a student names a change but not its effect, then offer 'This changes the story because...' Success: the student states one change and its effect using a frame."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: remembering what the film changed","tryThis":"Replay a short clip and have the student fill a two-column chart (book / film) with one detail each before speaking."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask the student to add a myth detail and explain how the three versions (myth, novel, film) each reflect a different generation or culture."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on their readiness for the academic discussion and name a next step.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-quick-write","title":"Quick Write: Discussion Ready","minutes":5,"standards":[],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Re-rate yourself on the three Launch statements. Then write two or three sentences: What is one point you will make in the discussion, and what evidence will you use?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is your point, and what evidence supports it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"My point is that Riordan's version of the Underworld is more modern than Virgil's. For example, the 'NO LIVING' sign and the guard in the lobby show it, whereas Virgil's crossing is dark and serious. I now feel ready to use a discourse marker when I explain it."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Invite two or three students to share. Note students who still need help with evidence or the novel-film comparison, and use that information in the next Flex Day, F4, or in small groups."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"This Flex Day gave students extra time and support to finish preparing for their academic discussion on how retellings change across cultures and generations. Three Huddles reteach citing specific evidence, using discourse markers and formal wording, and comparing the novel with the film.","keyActivities":["Launch: Discussion Check-In self-rating used to form Huddles","Huddle 1: Evidence from the Novel and Myths","Huddle 2: Language of Academic Discussion","Huddle 3: Comparing the Novel and the Film","Look Back: Quick Write on discussion readiness"],"vocabularyTaught":["retelling","adaptation","omit","perspective","discourse marker","faithful"],"standardsCovered":[]}}
